title: Words instead of bulls (Hosea 14:3)
hook: since the Temple fell, reading about the offerings stands in for them

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer that asks what are we, and answers: your people. Your line was small, yet loved. When did you feel both? Today, a part of the morning that surprises people who find it. Day five hundred fifty-one.

Open a traditional prayer book to the early morning pages and you'll find something surprising. Instructions for animal offerings. The daily lamb, morning and evening. The recipe for the Temple incense, ingredient by ingredient. Where in the Temple each offering was slaughtered. Rome destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem long ago, and there hasn't been one since. So why are these pages here, in a book people carry to work on the train? The answer starts with a prophet, and a strange phrase: the bulls of our lips.
screen: `OFFERINGS IN THE PRAYER BOOK.` → `NO TEMPLE, NO ALTAR.` → `THE BULLS OF OUR LIPS.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew word is korbanot, offerings, from a root that means to come near. An offering was a way of drawing close. When the Temple stood, priests offered a lamb every morning and every evening, the tamid, the constant offering. Then it was gone. How do you draw near without an altar? The rabbis found an answer in the prophet Hosea. In the old Jewish translation: "Take with you words, and return unto the LORD." And a few lines on: "so will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips." Words, standing where the bulls once stood. The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, tells a story. Abraham asks God: when my children have no Temple, how will they be forgiven? And God answers: I have already arranged for them the order of the offerings. Whenever they read it, I will count it as if they had brought them. So the prayer book prints the passages, and people read them. Jewish communities treat these pages differently today. Orthodox prayer books keep them, and many add prayers for the Temple's rebuilding. Reform prayer books generally removed them. Conservative prayer books have often kept some readings while recasting the requests as remembrance. Across those differences runs Hosea's idea: words can carry what used to be carried on an altar.
screen: `KORBANOT: COMING NEAR.` · `TAKE WITH YOU WORDS.` · `READ IT, AND IT COUNTS.` · `COMMUNITIES KEEP IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `WORDS INSTEAD OF OFFERINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say words in place of an offering. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you would give, if giving were simple: an apology you owe, a thank you you never said, a promise you want to make. In the old world it might have been a lamb. Here it's words. Shape them slowly, until they're true. Then say them, quietly, out loud. If you pray, you can offer them to God. If not, offer them to the person they belong to, in your mind, and maybe later in person. The bell holds the time.
Korbanot. Offerings, from the root for coming near. Since the Temple fell, the morning reading of them stands in their place.
Your line: words instead of offerings. Today, say the words you shaped to the person they belong to, in a call, a note or face to face. Day five hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Orthodox prayer books print the passages on the daily offering, the incense and the places of the offerings early in the morning service, and many people read them daily; other movements' prayer books shorten, recast or omit them.
